chapter_title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines

m1_zero_omission_notes.summary: This chapter explores the geometry of triangles formed by three intersecting lines. It establishes the Triangle Inequality Theorem, conditions for triangle existence, and classification of triangles based on side lengths.

detailed_sections.full_notes: When three lines intersect pairwise in a plane at three distinct points, they form a triangle. The three points of intersection are vertices, and the line segments connecting them are sides.

margin_notes.title: Direct vs Roundabout Path
margin_notes.content: The direct straight path between two points is always shorter than any roundabout path passing through a third point.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
Triangle Inequality Theorem: A triangle can exist if and only if the sum of the lengths of ANY two sides is strictly GREATER than the length of the third side.
Mathematical conditions for side lengths a, b, c:
1. a + b > c
2. b + c > a
3. c + a > b
Shortcut test: The sum of the two smaller side lengths must be strictly greater than the largest side length.

margin_notes.title: Quick Existence Check
margin_notes.content: Can sides be 3 cm, 3 cm, 7 cm? No, because 3 + 3 = 6 < 7.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
1. Equilateral Triangle: All three sides equal (a = b = c). An equilateral triangle of any positive side length always exists because a + a = 2a > a.
2. Isosceles Triangle: Two sides equal.
3. Scalene Triangle: All three sides unequal.

margin_notes.title: Equilateral Always Exists
margin_notes.content: For any side length s > 0, s + s = 2s > s is always true.

m2_key_terms_formulas_and_rules.definition_or_expression: a + b > c, b + c > a, c + a > b

m3_practical_activities_and_procedures.activity_title: Ruler and Compass Triangle Existence Construction
m3_practical_activities_and_procedures.aim: To attempt constructing triangles with given side lengths to test feasibility
procedure: Set compass to length a, draw arc from one endpoint.
Set compass to length b, draw arc from other endpoint.
m3_practical_activities_and_procedures.observation_and_conclusion: Arcs intersect only if a + b > c. If a + b <= c, arcs do not intersect, proving no triangle can be formed.

diagrams.instructions: Draw triangle ABC showing direct side AB = c and two-step path AC + CB = b + a.
diagrams.structural_details: Visualizes why straight path c < a + b.

end_exercises.question: Can 24, 26, 28 be side lengths of a triangle? Explain.
end_exercises.answer: Yes. Check: 24 + 26 = 50 > 28; 24 + 28 = 52 > 26; 26 + 28 = 54 > 24. Since the sum of any two sides is greater than the third, a triangle exists.

end_exercises.question: Check if a triangle exists for side lengths 3, 6, 9.
end_exercises.answer: Smallest sides sum = 3 + 6 = 9. Third side = 9. Since 9 is not strictly greater than 9 (9 = 9), a triangle CANNOT exist.

end_exercises.question: Does there exist an equilateral triangle with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, for any side length?
end_exercises.answer: Yes. 50 + 50 = 100 > 50. In general, for side length s > 0, s + s = 2s > s is always true for all positive numbers s. Thus, an equilateral triangle exists for any side length.

extract_based.extract_text: Is it possible to assign lengths 10 km, 10 km, 25 km to form a triangular path?

qa.question: Determine whether this triangular path is possible.
qa.answer: 10 + 10 = 20 km < 25 km. No, the path cannot form a closed triangle.

level_1_objective_1_mark.question: Which set of numbers can form the sides of a triangle?

level_2_short_answer_2_3_marks.question: Two sides of a triangle measure 6 cm and 10 cm. What is the range of possible lengths for the third side 'x'?
level_2_short_answer_2_3_marks.answer:
1. Upper limit: x < 6 + 10 => x < 16 cm.
2. Lower limit: x + 6 > 10 => x > 4 cm.
Range: 4 cm < x < 16 cm.

level_3_long_answer_5_marks.question: Test triangle existence for the following four side length sets with full step-by-step reasoning: (i) 1, 1, 5  (ii) 2, 4, 8  (iii) 10, 20, 25  (iv) 1, 100, 100.
level_3_long_answer_5_marks.answer:
(i) 1, 1, 5: 1 + 1 = 2 < 5 -> Triangle does NOT exist.
(ii) 2, 4, 8: 2 + 4 = 6 < 8 -> Triangle does NOT exist.
(iii) 10, 20, 25: 10 + 20 = 30 > 25 -> Triangle EXISTS.
(iv) 1, 100, 100: 1 + 100 = 101 > 100 -> Triangle EXISTS.

level_4_competency_case_study.scenario: A surveyor maps three towns A, B, C. Road AB = 12 km, Road BC = 20 km, Road AC = 40 km.

qa.question: The surveyor claims towns A, B, C form a triangle. Is the map accurate?
qa.answer: Check: AB + BC = 12 + 20 = 32 km. However, AC = 40 km. Since 32 < 40, towns A, B, C cannot form a triangle. The map claim is inaccurate.

m7_common_pitfalls.common_error: Checking only one pair of sides for the triangle inequality instead of the two smallest sides against the largest.
m7_common_pitfalls.correct_approach: Always identify the longest side and verify if the sum of the remaining two smaller sides strictly exceeds it.
